newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. race highlights language stakes.
newsitem.headline: U.N. race highlights language stakes.

text.p: Speculation that the contest for U.N. secretary-general might be developing into a "language war" heightened after inconclusive unofficial balloting on the four African candidates on Tuesday.
The only one from an English-speaking country, U.N. Under-Secretary-General Kofi Annan of Ghana, led the field with 10 votes in favour and four against.
But one of the negative votes in the secret ballot was cast by a veto-bearing permanent members of the Security Council and speculation focused on France.

The five permanent members of the council -- the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France -- use ballots which are different from those of the 10 non-permanent members who have no veto. The balloting resumes on Wednesday.

The other three candidates, all from Francophone African countries, received fewer votes than Annan and each drew the negative votes of two permanent council members. In their case, speculation centred on the United States and Britain.

The three hopefuls from French-speaking countries are: Amara Essy, the foreign minister of Ivory Coast, who presided over the 1994-95 session of the U.N. General Assembly; Hamid Algabid of Niger, a former prime minister and currently secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference; and Ahmedou Ould-Abdallah of Mauritania, a former foreign minister who now heads the Washington-based think-tank, the Global Coalition for Africa.
Essy received seven votes in favour and four against, including two by permanent council members.
Algabid's tally was five for and seven against, including two negative votes by permanent members, while Ould-Abdallah received three votes and seven against, including two by permanent members.
France has said it would veto any candidate whose command of French it considered inadequate.
Annan, who heads U.N. peacekeeping operations, speaks French, has worked for the United Nations in Geneva and studied there at the Institut Universitaire des Hautes Etudes Internationales.
He is widely considered the candidate most favoured by the United States.

France, for its part, is thought to resent the U.S. vetoing last month of the incumbent secretary-general, Boutros Boutros-Ghali, who had the support of all 14 other council members in a Nov. 19 vote in which he was the sole candidate.

Washington says the United Nations needs new leadership to carry out reforms. It also favours a candidate whose command of English would not only resonate among the largely English-speaking press corps in New York but influence a sceptical U.S. Congress.

Paris not only championed Boutros-Ghali's election for an initial five-year term in 1991 but was widely perceived as having used its influence to ensure his victory by out-manoeuvring other council members, including the United States and Britain.
Although Boutros-Ghali "suspended" his candidacy on Dec. 4 and did not figure in Tuesday's ballotting, he has not withdrawn from the race.

Any attempt to re-enter the contest is regarded as certain to draw another U.S. veto -- just as any candidate favoured by the United States could meet a similar fate at the hands of one or more of the council's other permanent members.
